newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK handover: mixed emotions for Overseas Chinese.
newsitem.headline: HK handover: mixed emotions for Overseas Chinese.

text.p: Millions of overseas Chinese, who feel home is where the heart is, view Britain's handover of Hong Kong to China with a mixture of political trepidation and economic optimism.
With the eyes of the world turning to Hong Kong on June 30, this is inevitably a time of reflection for the "bamboo network" of ethnic Chinese around the world from Vancouver to Melbourne.
They worry about everything from passports to human rights but believe China won't tamper with the laissez-faire economy that turned Hong Kong into a trading powerhouse.
The Chinese diaspora forms a powerful network of business contacts that could be a major factor as China's economy booms and foreign investment beckons.

"Ethnic Chinese will form the most powerful network of entrepreneurs in the next decade. Fifty-four million ethnic Chinese worldwide, with assets of more than one trillion dollars are the most successful entrepreneurs in the world," said John Naisbitt, author of "Megatrends Asia."
In London's Chinatown, Soho shopkeepers question China's human rights record after the Tiananmen Square crackdown but believe Hong Kong can survive as a humming capitalist dynamo.
Peter Wong, born in Hong Kong but brought up in England, said: "In mainland China, human rights are not as good as in Hong Kong. That is something I worry about."
Alan Lee agreed: "I was born in Hong Kong too. The Chinese give me no faith too. I don't feel comfortable at them taking it back from the British."

About three million of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people are eligible for a British travel document, a second-class passport which grants no residency rights in Britain but confers some consular protection and travel convenience.

About 750,000 people have foreign citizenship. Most made Canada, Australia or Britain their adopted homes. Under the post-1997 constitution, residents with foreign passports can retain right of abode but if they are abroad for too long after July 1, they might lose it.

Britain, the United States, Canada, Australia. Singapore, Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Turkey have recognised the new Special Administrative Region (SAR) passports now being introduced by Hong Kong.
The South China Morning Post, Hong Kong's flagship English-language paper, went on the international vox pop trail to see how overseas Chinese felt about the end of colonial rule.

Vancouver talk show host Hanson Lau said: "Ex-Hong Kong people are not too worried, they don't think it will make too much of a difference. We are not talking about Hong Kong being free but whether it will continue to prosper."

Melbourne lawyer Baptista Lai believed the economy would succeed because China wanted it to, but on human rights said: "If you are asking whether people would enjoy the same kind of freedoms, especially as a journalist like yourself, I would have doubts."

And that worry was echoed by Washington-based engineer Andrew Au. "I am happy to see China claim back the territory -- I have no problem with that -- but the problem is that Hong Kong is returning to a government that does not treat its people well," he said.
